episodes.title: The Invisible Universe: Dark Matter, the Higgs & Why We Exist | Marcela Carena
episodes.description:
Most of the universe is invisible. Yet the things we cannot see are responsible for much of the world we know. An invisible field gives fundamental particles their mass. Mysterious dark matter holds galaxies together. And a tiny imbalance between matter and antimatter may explain why we exist at all.

In this public lecture, Perimeter Institute Executive Director and theoretical physicist Marcela Carena takes us behind the scenes of the universe to explore some of the biggest mysteries in modern physics. From the Higgs boson and elusive neutrinos to dark matter and gravitational waves, Carena examines how scientists are searching for the invisible ingredients of our cosmos—and how discoveries at the Large Hadron Collider, underground laboratories, and gravitational-wave observatories could help reveal what happened in the first moments after the Big Bang.

About the Speaker

Marcela Carena is the Executive Director of Perimeter Institute for Theoretical Physics and an internationally recognized theoretical particle physicist. Previously the Director of the Theory Division at Fermi National Accelerator Laboratory (Fermilab), she is also a professor at the University of Chicago. Her research explores connections between the Higgs boson, dark matter, and the origin of matter in the universe, with a particular focus on how new particles and forces might be discovered through experiments such as CERN's Large Hadron Collider.

episodes.title: Curiosity and the Cosmos: CBC IDEAS at Perimeter Institute
episodes.description:
Math may be the language of the universe, and brilliant minds and technology may have unlocked many of the secrets of the cosmos. But the pursuit of knowledge and insight always begins with the same thing: Curiosity.

Join us for a special recording of CBC Radio’s IDEAS, featuring groundbreaking Perimeter Institute researcher Asimina Arvanitaki. In an adaptation of a talk she recently delivered in her native Greece, Asimina highlights the role curiosity has played in her own passion for science and in the history of scientific discovery. And in a wide-ranging chat with IDEAS host Nahlah Ayed, they cover such subjects as the importance of fundamental research, the responsibility of scientists to the public, and the role of AI in scientific research.

About CBC IDEAS:
IDEAS is a deep-dive into contemporary thought and intellectual history. Anchored in a powerful legacy and expansive archive spanning over five decades, its topics are boundless. The nature of consciousness. The history of toilets. The roots and rise of authoritarianism. Near death experiences. No idea is off-limits.

Each episode cracks open a concept to see how it's played out over place and time—and uncovers why it still matters today.

About Asimina Arvanitaki:
Asimina Arvanitaki (PhD Stanford University, 2008) is the Stavros Niarchos Foundation (SNF) Aristarchus Chair in Theoretical Physics at Perimeter Institute, where she has been a faculty member since 2014.

Asimina is a particle physicist whose work has focused on designing novel experiments that search for new phenomena and new forces of nature. She has shown, for example, how atomic clocks—the most precise time-keeping devices to date that are used to define the second and are responsible for the GPS that we all use—can be used to detect dark matter, the unknown mass component of our Cosmos that is responsible for the existence of galaxies.

She has also shown how black holes, such as those recently detected at the LIGO experiment, can be used to diagnose the presence of new particles. For her work, she was co-awarded the 2017 New Horizons in Physics Prize by the Breakthrough Prize Foundation. Recently, Asimina has received notable accolades, including the 2023 Loeb Lectures in Physics at Harvard University and the 2022 CAP-TRIUMF Vogt Medal from the Canadian Association of Physicists.

episodes.title: Interstellar Objects and the New Solar System | Chris Lintott
episodes.description:
In July 2025, astronomers detected something extraordinary: an object moving through our Solar System that came from somewhere else in the Milky Way.

3I/ATLAS is only the third interstellar object ever identified, and it may have formed more than 9 billion years ago — billions of years before the Sun and Earth existed. What can a visitor this ancient tell us about the history of our galaxy, the formation of planetary systems, and even the origins of our own Solar System?

In this lecture, Professor Chris Lintott explores the strange and surprising world of interstellar objects, from the mysterious ʻOumuamua to the comet Borisov and the remarkable discoveries surrounding 3I/ATLAS. He also explores what scientists are learning from the small bodies closer to home, including NASA’s OSIRIS-REx mission and its extraordinary sample return from asteroid Bennu.

These objects may be small, but they preserve clues to a much bigger story. Bennu contains complex chemistry, including amino acids, while observations of 3I/ATLAS are revealing information about the conditions that existed in the Milky Way billions of years ago.

And this may just be the beginning. The Vera C. Rubin Observatory is ushering in a new era of discovery, with the potential to find millions of new asteroids and perhaps 100–200 interstellar objects over the lifetime of its survey. Each could offer a new glimpse into a different place and time in our galaxy.

Professor Chris Lintott is a Professor of Astrophysics and Citizen Science Lead at the University of Oxford, a Research Fellow at New College, and a co-founder of Zooniverse. He is also the 39th Professor of Astronomy at Gresham College and a broadcaster for the BBC’s The Sky at Night.

episodes.title: Built by Physics. Built by Philanthropy.
episodes.description:
Perimeter Institute exists because one philanthropist believed that investing in knowledge and human potential could change the world. Since its founding by Mike Lazaridis, Perimeter has pursued that bold idea, giving exceptional minds the freedom to pursue fundamental discovery.

History shows that transformative technologies often grow from asking questions with no practical application in mind. Einstein did not set out to invent GPS, and the pioneers of quantum mechanics were not trying to create smartphones or MRI machines. They were seeking a deeper understanding of the world.

Today, Perimeter researchers are exploring profound questions about our universe. We cannot know where the next breakthrough will come from, but we do know that we must invest in curiosity and talent.
By supporting Perimeter, donors help create the conditions for discoveries that will shape the future.

Learn more: https://perimeterinstitute.ca/built-by-physics

episodes.title: Quantum Metrology: Pushing the Limits of Measurement | Sisi Zhou
episodes.description:
What could we discover if we could measure more precisely?

Perimeter Institute researcher Sisi Zhou explores quantum metrology—using quantum systems to make ultraprecise measurements—and explains how quantum error correction can reduce noise while preserving the signals researchers want to measure. 

From atomic clocks and gravitational-wave detection to the search for dark matter, Zhou discusses where quantum metrology could make a difference. She also explores a central challenge: turning theoretical promise into practical quantum sensors that outperform classical alternatives under real-world conditions.

The conversation also touches on AI’s changing role in theoretical research and why connecting ideas across physics, mathematics, computer science, and other disciplines matters for the future of quantum information science.

Read the full story here: https://perimeterinstitute.ca/news/future-physics-quantum-metrology

episodes.title: What is an imaginary number?
episodes.description:

Watch the full talk on our YouTube channel to hear Brown discuss recent progress in training AIs to do science and reasoning, and what it will mean for the future of physics if these trends continue.

episodes.title: What Does Quantum Cryptography Have to Do with Gravity? With Alex May
episodes.description:
Quantum gravity and quantum cryptography may seem like completely different fields, but they share a surprising connection.

In this 4-minute explainer, Alex May, Murray Gell-Mann Chair in Theoretical Physics at Perimeter Institute, introduces the AdS/CFT correspondence, a remarkable idea suggesting that gravity in a higher-dimensional spacetime can be equivalent to a quantum theory living on its lower-dimensional boundary.

One puzzle is how interactions that seem possible in the higher-dimensional gravitational picture can emerge from the lower-dimensional theory. As Alex explains, the answer comes from an unexpected place: quantum cryptography. By using protocols built on quantum entanglement, physicists can reproduce these interactions, revealing a deep connection between information, entanglement, and the nature of spacetime.

episodes.title: The Future of Quantum Computing with Michele Mosca
episodes.description:
Practical quantum computing is close. That brings opportunity, but also cybersecurity risks. Quantum cryptography expert Michele Mosca walks us through the state of the field.

Michele Mosca is a research associate faculty member at Perimeter Institute. He was one of the institute’s first researchers when it was launched 25 years ago. He is also a founder and former deputy director of the Institute for Quantum Computing at the University of Waterloo, where he is a mathematics professor. 

Mosca is a pioneer in the design of quantum algorithms, grappling with both the potential of quantum computers and the security challenges they pose. The first experimental implementation of a quantum algorithm on a physical system was achieved in 1998 by Mosca and Jonathan A. Jones at Oxford University. They successfully executed Deutsch's algorithm using a 2-qubit Nuclear Magnetic Resonance (NMR) quantum computer.

In 2018, Mosca devised a risk framework designed to help organizations determine when they need to transition to quantum-safe encryption. Mosca has also launched several start-ups based on his research, and currently leads the quantum-safe cybersecurity company, evolutionQ.

We sat down with Mosca to talk about the state of quantum computing, the development of quantum error correction codes, threats to national security in the quantum computing era, and how Perimeter Institute can play a role in both the development of quantum computers and in ensuring a quantum-safe future.

episodes.title: How important is the cosmological constant?
episodes.description:
One number may have determined whether galaxies could exist at all.
Physicist Asimina Arvanitaki explains that if the cosmological constant were only 10 times larger, galaxies could have been torn apart before they ever formed.
No galaxies. No stars. No life.
A reminder of how finely balanced our universe really is.

episodes.title: When a physicist is asked what their favourite number is
episodes.description:

🌙 Moon = ~400× smaller than the Sun
☀️ Sun = ~400× farther away

And that's why they appear almost exactly the same size in our sky during an eclipse.

episodes.title: Training Sand to Think: Artificial General Intelligence & Future of Physics
episodes.description:
Our civilization has learned how to turn sand into silicon chips, silicon chips into neural networks, and neural networks into Artificial Intelligences (AIs). Over the last half-decade, the capabilities of large language model AIs (like ChatGPT and Gemini) have leapt from babbling preschoolers to International Math Olympiad gold medalists, and now beyond. This talk reviews recent progress in training AIs to do science and reasoning, and speculates as to what it will mean for the future of physics if these trends continue.

About the Speaker

Adam Brown leads Blueshift—a research team at Google DeepMind focused on advancing the scientific and reasoning capabilities of artificial intelligence—and is a core contributor to Gemini. Before Google, he studied physics and philosophy at Oxford, earned a PhD at Columbia, and subsequently held academic positions in the physics departments at Princeton and Stanford. There he taught Einstein’s general theory of relativity and conducted research on topics spanning the big bang, inflation, the multiverse, black holes, quantum computation, space elevators, bubbles of nothing, and the long-term fate of the universe, as well as the deep connections between physics and computer science. He joined Google in 2018.

episodes.title: CBC IDEAS at Perimeter - The Numbers That Shape Our Universe
episodes.description:
From π to the speed of light, from Planck’s constant to a physicist’s personal “favourite number”, some numbers do far more than describe the universe - they help define it. But what do these numbers actually mean? Why do they matter? And what would the universe look like if they were even slightly different?

In this special episode recording of CBC IDEAS, three Perimeter Institute researchers (Ben Webster, Matthew Johnson, and Mina Arvanitaki) explore the fundamental numbers behind reality. Through a mix of fast-paced lightning rounds and deeper reflections, the conversation brings together vivid explanations, surprising stories, humour, and those unforgettable moments of awe that reveal just how strange - and beautiful - our universe really is.

episodes.title: How is AI being used in physics today?
episodes.description:
Artificial intelligence is transforming physics, and reshaping how discoveries are made.

Long before tools like ChatGPT became widely known, physicists were already using AI to tackle some of the most complex problems in science. Today, AI is helping researchers simulate quantum systems, analyze massive datasets, and even model the behaviour of quantum computers.

In this conversation, physicist Roger Melko explores how AI is changing the way physics is done, and what it means for the future of scientific discovery.

episodes.title: Mayuko Yamashita: Translator of the universal language
episodes.description:
Mayuko Yamashita has been listening to the language of mathematics since childhood. Drawn early to puzzles and deep logical structures, she competed in Japan’s Mathematical Olympiad, where conversations with older students opened her eyes to a richer world of mathematical thought. After completing her master’s and PhD in Tokyo and spending six years at Kyoto University, she arrived at Perimeter Institute in 2025 with what she calls a “pure mathematical mind,” ready to explore how that language resonates across physics.

Yamashita, who holds the Hideki Yukawa Chair in Theoretical Physics, works at Perimeter amid a chorus of scientific dialects, from quantum gravity to astrophysics, embracing the challenge of translating between them. Using tools such as homotopy theory, she helps determine whether mathematically elegant physical theories are also internally consistent, acting as a bridge between mathematical rigour and physical intuition. Supported by an environment that encourages bold, cross‑disciplinary exploration, she seeks the unexpected connections where new discoveries are most likely to emerge.

episodes.title: Rob Spekkens: a detective descrambling reality
episodes.description:
Rob Spekkens describes his work as “unscrambling an omelet,” separating two ideas long mixed together in quantum theory: what actually exists and what we can know about it. Trained in both physics and philosophy, he has always focused on “why questions,” pushing beyond the idea that it’s enough for quantum theory to simply work without being fully understood.

Using simplified toy models and tools from causal inference, Spekkens shows that some quantum strangeness may come from limits on knowledge rather than from reality itself. At Perimeter Institute, he approaches physics like a detective—untangling cause from coincidence in hopes of gaining a clearer understanding of quantum theory more than a century after its discovery.

episodes.title: Ka'satstenhera – Unity of Hearts and Minds by Jay Havens | Perimeter Institute Public Lecture
episodes.description:
Artist Jay Havens explores local Haudenosaunee cultural and art history, and the theme of Ka'satsténhsera – Unity of Hearts and Minds.

This talk places Jay's artwork for the Perimeter Institute in context, discussing Haudenosaunee history here on the Haldimand tract, including contemporary Haudenosaunee culture on Six Nations. The talk describes the history of the Woodland school of art, as well as discussing the Indigenous Group of Seven, to show the development of the art style that Jay works in.

episodes.title: Luis Lehner: Decoding the universe’s hidden messages
episodes.description:
Luis Lehner learned early that the most interesting things are the ones you can’t quite see. As a toddler in Argentina, he would open every kitchen drawer he could find—not to cause trouble, but simply to discover what was just out of sight. That instinctive curiosity never left him. Today, as a theoretical physicist, Lehner, who holds the Carlo Fidani Rainer Weiss Chair in Theoretical Physics at Perimeter, studies extreme cosmic environments where black holes and neutron stars collide so violently that the resulting ripples in spacetime can be detected on Earth.

For most of astronomy’s history, light was our main “messenger,” but now scientists can also learn from neutrinos and gravitational waves—signals that carry information from places light can’t escape. Lehner vividly remembers LIGO’s first confirmed detection in 2015, when he and colleagues listened to the telltale “chirp” and felt a new era begin. His drive to learn still propels him—whether he’s unraveling physics mysteries or flying airplanes, where full focus is non-negotiable.

episodes.title: William East: Exploring the places where gravity breaks
episodes.description:
When black holes collide, they shake the universe itself.

These cosmic collisions send ripples through spacetime known as gravitational waves, a phenomenon predicted by Albert Einstein more than a century ago and first detected in 2015 by the LIGO observatory. That discovery marked the birth of a new kind of astronomy.

For William East, faculty member at Perimeter Institute for Theoretical Physics, it marked the beginning of a frontier he was eager to explore.

episodes.title: Lucien Hardy: A quarter-century exploring physics frontiers
episodes.description:
Lucien Hardy arrived in Waterloo 25 years ago with no intention of leaving Oxford, but persistent invitations — and a plane ticket from colleague Michele Mosca — drew him to a fledgling research institute operating out of an old post office. There he found a small group of physicists committed to the idea that breakthroughs come from collaboration, paradoxes, and the freedom to chase bold ideas. Captivated by the vision and backing behind founder Mike Lazaridis’s plan, Hardy joined the effort, shifting not only countries but also his research focus.

Already known for foundational work like “Hardy’s Paradox,” he increasingly pursued an axiomatic approach to quantum theory and turned toward the major open challenge in physics: unifying quantum mechanics with general relativity. At Perimeter, he has spent two decades developing new frameworks that allow for radical possibilities, including the idea that even causal order may be indefinite in quantum gravity. Though the work is often baffling, Hardy thrives in Perimeter’s collaborative environment and marvels at how it has grown from a group of renegades in a repurposed post office to the world’s largest — and, to him, best — theoretical physics institute.

episodes.title: Neal Dalal: Sharpening our View of the Universe
episodes.description:
What if we could take a high-definition portrait of a black hole?

Perimeter Institute researcher Neal Dalal believes we’re closer than ever.

Black holes are the most elusive objects in the universe, swallowing light, hiding behind event horizons, and revealing themselves only through the chaos swirling around them. In 2019, the Event Horizon Telescope captured the first-ever image of a black hole: a fuzzy orange ring that stunned the world.

Dalal wants to go thousands of times sharper.

His career spans neutrinos, cosmic structure, and dark matter. Now, he’s pushing the boundaries of what’s technologically possible and challenging the world to imagine a new era of astronomical imaging.

episodes.title: Katie Mack: Exploring gravity in mind and body
episodes.description:
Katie Mack, a cosmologist and aviator, has found two passions that perfectly complement each other — studying the universe and flying through the sky. What began as a hobby during the pandemic became a defining part of her life. In physics, she explores gravity’s mysteries; in flight, she feels its pull firsthand. As the inaugural Hawking Chair in Cosmology and Science Communication, she divides her time between researching the universe’s origins and explaining those ideas to the public, continuing Stephen Hawking’s legacy of making cosmology accessible and inspiring.

Mack’s talent for communication shines through her video series _Quantum 101_ and _Cosmology 101_ which make complex physics understandable through clear explanations and creative metaphors. Her first book, _The End of Everything: Astrophysically Speaking_ earned wide praise for blending humour and insight in describing the universe’s possible fates. Her next book turns to the smallest scales of existence, exploring the nature of particles and reality itself.

Driven by deep curiosity, Mack studies topics from cosmic inflation to dark matter, always seeking to understand how everything began — and how it might end. Flying gives her the same sense of wonder she finds in cosmology, offering focus, freedom, and awe. Whether gazing into the depths of space or soaring through clouds, Mack is united by a single goal: to explore the infinite, both above and beyond.

episodes.title: 100 Years of Quantum: Perspectives on its Past, Present, and Future
episodes.description:
In July 1925, on the island of Helgoland, Werner Heisenberg made a breakthrough that ultimately led to modern quantum theory.

100 years later, physicists are still grappling with what it means.

This panel discussion brought together experts in the history and philosophy of physics alongside researchers in quantum foundations to explore the past, present, and future of quantum theory. The diverse perspectives of the panellists promise a dynamic and engaging exploration of the most profound and puzzling topics in physics today.

episodes.title: Junwu Huang: Unraveling the Mystery of Dark Matter
episodes.description:
What is dark matter, and how can we find it?

For Perimeter Institute physicist Junwu Huang, that question sits at the heart of his research. A theorist with a restless curiosity, Huang develops ideas that could help experimental physicists detect the invisible matter shaping our universe.

Born and raised in Hangzhou, China, Huang followed his fascination with physics from Beijing to Stanford, where he trained under particle theorist Savas Dimopoulos. He joined Perimeter as a postdoctoral researcher in 2017 and became faculty in 2020, drawn by the Institute’s culture of bold, interdisciplinary exploration.

At Perimeter, Huang thrives at the intersection of theory and experiment — a place where ideas can leap from blackboards to laboratories. His work narrows the vast possibilities of what dark matter could be, pointing the way for discoveries that could reshape our understanding of the cosmos.

episodes.title: CBC Radio Quirks & Quarks: 50th Anniversary Episode at Perimeter Institute
episodes.description:
On October 9, 1975, CBC listeners across the country heard David Suzuki introduce the very first episode of Quirks & Quarks. 50 years and thousands of interviews later, Quirks is still going strong, bringing wonders from the world of science to listeners, old and new.

On Oct 7, 2025, we’ll be celebrating with a birthday show in front of a live audience at the Perimeter Institute for Theoretical Physics in Waterloo, Ontario. We’ll have guests from a range of scientific disciplines looking at what we’ve learned in the last 50 years, and hazarding some predictions about what the next half century could hold.

We’ll hear about revolutions in cosmology like the discovery of dark matter and dark energy and the observation of black holes, and whether we’ll understand where the universe came from. We’ll explore how we successfully fed a population of 8 billion people, and how we’ll feed the teeming masses of the future without exhausting our planet. We’ll look at the past and future of the technology that has transformed our world and the future of AI that, it seems, may transform it further. And there will be much, much more.

QUIRKS & QUARKS is an award-winning weekly radio science program, also heard around the world via its weekly podcast. For 50 years, it has brought its listeners to the cutting edge of scientific inquiry. Hosted by Bob McDonald, the program presents the people behind the latest discoveries in the physical and natural sciences, from the smallest sub-atomic particle to the largest objects in the sky and everything in between. It also examines the political, social, environmental and ethical implications of new developments in science and technology.

About the Host

Bob McDonald has been communicating science internationally through television, radio, print and live presentations for more than 40 years. He is the host of CBC Radio's QUIRKS & QUARKS, the award-winning science program with a national audience of nearly 500,000 people. He is also a regular reporter for CBC Television's THE NATIONAL as well as Gemini-winning host and writer of the children's series Heads Up! McDonald has also hosted The Greatest Canadian Invention and the seven-part series Water Under Fire.

As a print journalist, McDonald has authored four science books and contributed to numerous science textbooks, newspapers and magazines including The Globe and Mail, Owl Magazine and many others. His latest book is Canadian Spacewalkers: Hadfield MacLean and Williams Remember The Ultimate High Adventure. He wrote the introduction to The Quirks & Quarks Question Book and the Guide to Space: 42 Questions (and Answers) About Life, the Universe, and Everything.

Beyond his work in media, McDonald sits on the board of Friends of the Dominion Astrophysical Observatory, and is in demand as a public speaker across the country.

McDonald has been honoured for his outstanding contribution to the promotion of science in Canada as the recipient of the Michael Smith Award from the Natural Sciences and Engineering Research Council, the Sir Sanford Fleming Medal from the Royal Canadian Institute and the McNeil Medal from The Royal Society of Canada. McDonald was also the recipient of a 2008 Gemini Award for Best Host in a Pre-School, Children's or Youth Program or Series.

He has received twelve honourary Doctorates, and two honourary college degrees. In 2011 he was appointed an Officer of the Order of Canada, and in 2014, asteroid 2006 XN67 was officially named bobmcdonald in his honour.

episodes.title: Can We Test if Gravity Is Quantum?
episodes.description:
For so long, quantum gravity has been led by theory.

But what if small, carefully designed tabletop experiments could finally test whether gravity is truly a quantum force?


In this clip, a Stanford PhD student shares why this shift from theory to experiment is one of the most exciting developments for the future of quantum information and quantum gravity. While the challenge requires intense quantum control and extremely precise measurements, it is not beyond reach, it’s an engineering problem.


These potential experiments could fundamentally reshape our understanding of gravity and guide us toward whether a fully quantum theory of gravity is the right path, or whether something else, perhaps a quantum-classical theory, is needed.

episodes.title: Heat Death: The Cold, Dark, Lonely End to the Universe #astrophysics
episodes.description: Astrophysicist Katie Mack explains the concept of heat death, the most likely fate of our universe. Despite the name, heat death isn’t fiery — it’s a cold, desolate ending often called the Big Freeze. As entropy spreads and the universe expands, everything drifts further apart until no usable energy remains. Katie walks through how astronomers discovered in the 1990s that the universe isn’t slowing down but actually accelerating in its expansion — a strange result that makes heat death the leading theory for how it all ends.

episodes.title: Katie Mack on How the Universe Ends | Perimeter Institute Public Lecture
episodes.description:
The Big Bang theory tells the story of the beginning of the Universe, our cosmic home for the last 13.8 billion years. But how does the story end? I’ll share what modern astrophysics tells us about the ultimate fate of the cosmos, and what the catastrophic destruction of all reality would look like to anyone still around to see it.

Dr. Katie Mack is a theoretical astrophysicist exploring a range of questions in cosmology, the study of the universe from beginning to end. She currently holds the position of Hawking Chair in Cosmology and Science Communication at the Perimeter Institute for Theoretical Physics, where she carries out research on dark matter and the early universe and works to make physics more accessible to the general public. 

She is the author of the book "The End of Everything (Astrophysically Speaking)" and has written for a number of popular publications, such as the New York Times, Washington Post, Scientific American, Slate, Sky & Telescope, BBC Science Focus, and Cosmos magazine. You can read more about Dr. Mack and her work at www.astrokatie.com.
